blocks.title: Principle of superposition
blocks.text: If a particle of the medium is simultaneously acted upon by two waves, the resultant displacement of the particle is the algebraic sum of their individual displacements. In other words, the displacements of the individual waves are added together to form a new wave pattern (Fig. 7.4).

items: If two waves which overlap each other have the same phase, their resultant displacement is y = y1 + y2, where y1 and y2 are the displacements due to wave 1 and wave 2 and y is the resultant. In particular, if y1 = y2, the resultant displacement is y = 2 y1, or y = 2 y2 (Fig. 7.4a).
If two waves which cross each other have opposite phase, their resultant displacement is y = y1 + (-y2), or y = y1 - y2. In particular, if y1 = y2, the resultant displacement is y = 0 (Fig. 7.4b).

blocks.alt: Three rows. A red wave 1 and a blue wave 2 of the same wavelength and amplitude, with crests in line. Below them the purple resultant has twice the amplitude. The caption says crest meets crest and the amplitude doubles.
blocks.caption: Two waves in phase add up (constructive) (original diagram after Figure 7.4a).

blocks.text: Thus, if a particle of a medium is simultaneously acted upon by n waves such that its displacements due to each of the individual n waves are y1, y2, ..., yn, the resultant displacement y of the particle under the simultaneous action of these n waves is the algebraic sum of all the displacements: y = y1 + y2 + ... + yn. This is the principle of superposition of waves. Mathematically it can also be written as y(x,t) = y1(x,t) + y2(x,t) + ... + yn(x,t), where y(x,t) is the resultant wave, whereas y1(x,t), y2(x,t), ..., yn(x,t) are the individual waves; in the context of waves y(x,t) is the wave function or wave displacement at a given point x and time t, which describes the shape of the wave and its evolution over time. The principle of superposition applies to linear waves, or waves of small amplitude.

blocks.text: Applications of the principle of superposition
By applying the principle of superposition of waves, noise-cancelling headphones effectively eliminate unwanted noise, providing a more immersive and peaceful listening experience:

items: The headphones contain one or more microphones that capture ambient noise, such as background chatter, engine rumble or any environmental noise.
The microphone sends the sound signals to an amplifier and a processing unit in the headphones.
The processing unit generates an anti-noise signal, which is the exact opposite of the ambient noise in terms of amplitude and phase.
The anti-noise signal is then played through the headphones, along with the desired audio such as music or voice.
When the anti-noise signal meets the ambient noise, the two waves cancel each other out, resulting in a much quieter listening experience.

blocks.alt: Three rows. A red wave 1 and a blue wave 2 of the same wavelength and amplitude, with each crest of one opposite a trough of the other. Below them the purple resultant is a flat line. The caption says crest meets trough and the waves cancel.
blocks.caption: Two waves in opposite phase cancel (destructive) (original diagram after Figure 7.4b).

blocks.text: Though this is an oversimplification, since noise-cancelling headphones use complex algorithms and multiple microphones to achieve optimal cancellation, the basic principle of superposition remains fundamental to understanding how they work. An interference pattern formed with white light is shown in the Ponder Upon box.
